Severe Flooding Hits Taiwan’s Hospitality Industry: Hotels and Resorts Face Major Disruptions

TAICHUNG — Torrential rains triggered by a slow-moving tropical storm have caused extensive flooding across central and southern Taiwan this week, impacting numerous hotels, resorts, and other hospitality sites. As the storm continues to drench the region, industry leaders report ongoing damage to properties, loss of revenue, and significant challenges for thousands of workers.

According to the Taiwan Hospitality Association, more than 90 hotels and resorts in low-lying and coastal areas have experienced flooding of guest rooms, lobbies, kitchens, and recreational facilities. Popular destinations in Nantou, Chiayi, and Tainan counties have been among those hardest hit, with water levels rising above one meter in some properties. 

“The river burst its banks early Tuesday morning, and by noon our entire ground floor was under water,” said Lin Yu-fang, general manager of Lotus Springs Resort in Tainan County. “We evacuated all guests safely, but the damage to our facilities is severe. Our staff have been working around the clock to salvage what we can.”

Industry representatives say the storm struck at a crucial time, with many properties at near-full occupancy due to the summer holiday season. “In the past three days, we have received dozens of calls from member hotels reporting flooded basements, damaged electrical systems, and ruined furnishings,” said Chou Ming-liang, spokesperson for the Taiwan Hospitality Association. “The financial impact is already in the tens of millions of New Taiwan dollars, and the rain is not letting up.”

The flooding has forced the full or partial closure of more than 40 hotels and resorts, leaving hundreds of workers temporarily unable to perform their duties. Some staff have been reassigned to emergency response and cleanup efforts, while others have been sent home or placed on standby. “Our priority is the safety of our employees,” said Huang Mei-hua, HR manager at Sun River Hotel Group. “We’re providing temporary shelter and meals for staff whose own homes have also been affected.”

Union officials are calling for urgent support. “The hospitality workforce is under immense pressure, with many facing lost income and uncertainty about when they can return to work,” said Tsai Chien-hsiu, chairperson of the National Hospitality Workers Union. “We urge employers and authorities to ensure fair treatment and swift assistance for all affected staff.”

With meteorologists forecasting continued rainfall over the next 48 hours, hospitality operators are bracing for further disruption. The Taiwan Hospitality Association has established an emergency hotline to coordinate support for affected sites and workers as the crisis unfolds.
